title: Sublattice-selective control of spin reversal in metasurface-coupled Kagome interfaces
authors: Ximo Wang, Qiwei Han, Zhenqi Bai, Ruyue Guo, Min Feng, Yichi Zhang
abstract: Coherent manipulation of photonic interface states requires a control field that matches their internal mode structure. We study this requirement in a two-component Kagome lattice motivated by photon-mediated exchange near a nonlinear nonlocal metasurface. The Dirac spinors show why uniform Raman control cannot couple opposite-spin, same-valley interface modes at leading order, even when their spatial envelopes coincide. A $1:1:-2$ sublattice pattern removes this cancellation and maximizes the projected coupling at fixed root-mean-square amplitude within the diagonal-control class. We test this control scheme through full-zone topology and complete lattice propagation. For a smooth, gapped interface, a $720$-dimensional calculation gives target-mode fidelity $0.999937$ with leakage $6.27\times10^{-5}$ at RMS drive $0.04t$. Trace-preserving dynamics gives the separate survival condition needed for successful conversion. An exploratory three-dimensional lithium-niobate supercell reproduces the complex addressing pattern with $0.373\%$ relative error and provides nonlocal exchange, decay and electro-optic frequency-conversion matrices. The mode-resolved control principle thus gives quantitative electromagnetic design targets; the full spin-dependent device realization still requires further calibration.
summary: This research develops a method for precisely controlling spin reversal in photonic interface states within a Kagome lattice structure. By analyzing the coupling mechanisms, the authors determined that a specific sublattice pattern ($1:1:-2$) is required to overcome inherent symmetries that cause coupling cancellation. The findings provide quantitative electromagnetic design targets for realizing such spin-dependent quantum control in metasurface-coupled systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving sublattice-selective control for spin reversal in photonic interface states, overcoming limitations where uniform control fields fail to couple opposite-spin, same-valley modes.
main_result: An optimal sublattice pattern, specifically $1:1:-2$, was identified to maximize the projected coupling, achieving a high target-mode fidelity of $0.999937$ in full-zone topology calculations.
method: The study combines theoretical analysis of lattice Hamiltonians with numerical simulations, including full-zone topology calculations and an exploratory 3D supercell model.
model_or_system: The system is a two-component Kagome lattice motivated by photon-mediated exchange near a nonlinear nonlocal metasurface. The dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian and analyzed using projected Rabi amplitudes.
key_observables: Target-mode fidelity, leakage probability, projected Rabi amplitude ($\Omega_e$), and spin populations.
important_parameters: RMS drive amplitude ($0.04t$), sublattice pattern coefficients ($1, 1, -2$), and the lattice hopping terms ($t$).
main_assumptions: The derived control principle provides quantitative electromagnetic design targets, but the full spin-dependent device realization requires further calibration and assumptions about material constants are made in the EM tests.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the electric field magnitude, Raman-product phase, coherent exchange, and decay across the lattice structure in an exploratory COMSOL supercell.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the fundamental coupling limitations of uniform control to deriving the optimal sublattice pattern ($1:1:-2$), validating this pattern through full-zone topology calculations, and finally demonstrating the principle using an exploratory 3D supercell simulation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it merges concepts from topological photonics, open quantum systems (Lindblad dynamics), and structured light-matter interaction, providing concrete, quantifiable design rules for controlling quantum states in engineered photonic environments.
